payload.problem_addressed: How different components of distribution shift (geometry vs. modeled-physics change) separately and jointly affect the sample-efficiency benefit of pretraining a neural PDE surrogate before fine-tuning on a new target distribution.
payload.method_summary: Pretrain a convolutional U-Net surrogate on 254,909 RANS airfoil solutions from one geometry family (FT, SA closure), then fine-tune on a geometrically disjoint target family under two settings that share the same freestream ranges: same SA closure (geometry shift only) vs. SA plus an eN transition model (geometry + physics shift). Sample-efficiency gain is read off by comparing the fine-tuned model's error-vs-budget curve to a from-scratch control trained identically on the same target samples; breadth (many airfoils, few conditions each) vs. depth (few airfoils, many conditions) data allocation is also varied at fixed budget.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces a controlled experimental design that isolates one distribution-shift component at a time (geometry, then geometry+modeled-physics) rather than conflating multiple shifts, unlike prior PDE-pretraining evaluations. It shows that pretraining's sample-efficiency gain over training from scratch is not a fixed discount for distribution shift: the gain ordering between the two shift settings reverses as the target-data budget grows (favoring the harder shift at larger budgets), and that spreading a fixed budget across more distinct geometries (vs. more conditions per geometry) amplifies the pretraining gain only when the shift does not also change the modeled physics.
key_architecture_choices: Convolutional U-Net backbone (GroupNorm, GELU), selected over Transolver, ViT, FNO, and CViT at a matched ~22M-parameter budget for best accuracy at low training cost
Backbone fixed across all transfer experiments; only initialization/trainable-parameter set changes between pretraining, from-scratch, and fine-tuning runs
Geometry-disjoint train/val/test split (whole airfoils, not individual samples) so evaluation measures generalization to unseen shape rather than interpolation
datasets: UniFoil: FT airfoils (SA closure, pretraining source, 254,909 train samples)
UniFoil: NLF-Turb target (NLF airfoils, same SA closure -- geometry shift only)
UniFoil: NLF-Trans target (NLF airfoils, SA + eN transition model -- geometry + modeled-physics shift)
metrics: Field relative-L2 error over (u, v, Ma, Cp)
payload.headline_results: At N=1000 target samples, pretraining matches from-scratch accuracy trained on 3.25x as many samples for the same-closure geometry-shift target, and 2.58x as many for the geometry+transition-modeling target; by N=5000 the ordering reverses (1.56x vs. 1.86x). At N=1000, allocating the budget across more distinct airfoils (breadth) raises the geometry-shift gain from 3.3x to 4.0x but only marginally changes the transition-modeled gain (2.6x to 2.7x).
claimed_advantages: A frozen-backbone parallel convolutional adapter (+5% params) recovers 83% of full fine-tuning's improvement over the from-scratch control, at a fraction of the trainable-parameter cost

Pretraining removes one source of run-to-run variance: the fine-tuned model's error range across model-initialization seeds is markedly narrower than the from-scratch control's range on the same metric
Breadth (more distinct geometries) gives lower held-out error than depth (more conditions per geometry) for both targets at a fixed budget
limitations: Output recalibration alone is insufficient to bridge the shift: normalization-and-head fine-tuning (0.05% of weights) is no better than training from scratch, worse in three of four target-allocation cells

Findings are demonstrated on a single architecture (U-Net) and a single application domain (2D airfoil RANS aerodynamics); backbone selection used no target data but generalization of the shift-component ordering to other architectures is left open
Gains from pretraining shrink substantially as the fine-tuning budget grows, and the crossing point between the two shift-setting gain curves is bracketed (N=1000 to N=5000) but not resolved
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The paper's core methodology -- decomposing a domain gap into separate shift components (here: geometry vs. modeled physics) and measuring how the sample-efficiency benefit of pretraining/synthetic data depends jointly on target-budget size and target-data diversity -- is directly transferable to our own synthetic-inverse-factory-to-real-CAD domain gap: we could similarly vary 'shift components' one at a time (e.g. construction-template distribution vs. face-count/topology distribution) to decompose why hexgen underperforms on real CAD parts. The breadth-vs-depth finding (spend a limited real-CAD fine-tuning budget on more distinct parts rather than more programs per part, unless it will not resolve a physics/template mismatch) is a concrete, low-cost experimental-design lesson for how we allocate real-CAD auto-labeled fine-tuning data. The frozen-backbone adapter result (83% of full fine-tuning gain at 5% extra params) also suggests a cheap way to re-target a pretrained hexgen encoder-decoder to a new part family without full retraining.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a workshop paper (Representations for the Physical Sciences) evaluated on 2D airfoil RANS surrogates with a single architecture family (U-Net) held fixed across the transfer sweep, so the generality of the shift-component ordering across architectures/domains is unverified. No code link is given in the excerpted text. The central lesson -- pretraining value is a joint function of target-data budget, target-data diversity, and source-target physics/distribution mismatch, not a fixed discount -- is a useful experimental-design template to borrow even though the domain (CFD surrogates) is unrelated to CAD/meshing.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: S (adopting the shift-decomposition + breadth/depth ablation methodology for our own domain-gap diagnostics; no code or architecture reuse)
dependencies_on_other_methods: Parallel convolutional adapter for frozen-backbone transfer (Chen et al. 2024, Conv-Adapter)

payload.problem_addressed: Neural implicit 3D reconstruction methods (occupancy networks, NeRF, DeepSDF, NeuS, etc.) encode geometry in opaque high-dimensional latent parameters, limiting interpretability, geometric traceability, and direct reuse of reconstructed geometry within CAD/engineering workflows.
payload.method_summary: A hybrid neuro-symbolic pipeline: Phase I projects an unorganized point cloud onto the three principal orthographic planes, recovers watertight regions, and fits each with a NeuSOGA symbolic implicit-spline contour; the three view fields are fused via a shape-preserving constructive-solid-geometry (CSG) softMin operator (built from a compactly-supported R-function blend) into a coarse visual-hull hypothesis. Phase II decomposes the point cloud into dense cross-sectional slices along all three axes, fits each slice with a symbolic implicit contour, lofts each axis's slices into a continuous volumetric field using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines (PSPS, non-negative partition-of-unity basis functions derived from a smooth piecewise-polynomial transition function family), and fuses the three axis-wise volumetric hypotheses via the same shape-preserving CSG operator into the final reconstruction. The only learned component is a pretrained Segment Anything Model used upstream (inherited from NeuSOGA) for perceptual priors; the entire reconstruction process itself is deterministic symbolic geometry.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes NeuSOGA3D, a neuro-symbolic 3D reconstruction framework that restricts learning to perceptual abstraction and performs the actual geometric reconstruction through explicit, deterministic symbolic operators (implicit splines, PSPS volumetric lofting, and shape-preserving CSG), so every intermediate structure (contours, control polygons, cross-sections, CSG operators) remains inspectable and directly reusable as B-splines, NURBS surfaces, or boundary-representation (B-Rep) models. It also introduces a localized, compactly-supported R-function blending operator that suppresses the volumetric swelling and global distortion common in classical CSG blending. The framework is demonstrated across all 40 ModelNet40 categories without any category-specific training.
key_architecture_choices: Only the observation/perception module (a pretrained Segment Anything Model, inherited from prior NeuSOGA work) is learned; all downstream reconstruction is deterministic symbolic math
Multi-view orthographic projection (top/front/side) fused via shape-preserving CSG for a coarse visual hull
Multi-axial (x/y/z) dense cross-sectional decomposition, each axis lofted independently via Partial Shape-Preserving Splines, then fused via the same shape-preserving CSG consensus operator
Compactly-supported soft-absolute-value / softMin2 R-function blending operator in place of classical asymptotic R-functions to avoid volumetric inflation
datasets: ModelNet40 (all 40 categories, used for qualitative evaluation)
payload.headline_results: Experimental evaluation across all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrates the framework's generality and its ability to recover structurally meaningful, CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations; no quantitative reconstruction-accuracy numbers against baseline CAD-reconstruction methods are reported in the paper text.
claimed_advantages: Fully deterministic and analytically interpretable at every pipeline stage, unlike neural implicit methods whose geometry is opaque latent parameters
Extracted symbolic control structures are directly reusable across CAD paradigms (B-splines, NURBS, B-Rep, functional representations) without retraining, remeshing, or reverse engineering
Shape-preserving CSG blending avoids the volumetric swelling and global distortion of classical asymptotic R-function blending
Requires no category-specific training or learned geometric embeddings to generalize across all 40 ModelNet40 categories
limitations: Fine-scale geometric details and sharp structural transitions may be smoothed due to finite cross-sectional sampling and the current C1 continuity constraint on volumetric reconstruction
No quantitative comparison against learned CAD-reconstruction baselines (e.g. BRepNet, Point2CAD, CAD-Recode, BrepGen) is presented in the paper text -- evaluation is qualitative/visual
Released as an arXiv preprint explicitly flagged by the authors as unreviewed and subject to revision
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: This is a reverse-engineering direction (point cloud -> symbolic CAD structures) rather than our forward direction (B-rep -> hex-mesh program), but the underlying toolkit is relevant to our B-rep/CAD-representation-learning and structural-validity care areas: their deterministic, verifiable pipeline for turning geometric observations into explicit, CAD-compatible control structures (B-splines/NURBS/B-Rep) is a template for producing structurally-guaranteed-valid intermediate geometric representations, and their shape-preserving CSG blending operator (a compactly-supported R-function softMin) could be a useful deterministic primitive if hexgen or its verifier ever needs to compose or check solid-geometry operations symbolically rather than only via the downstream mesher. It's also a relevant related-work/contrast point: an alternative, fully-symbolic (non-autoregressive-decoder) philosophy for guaranteeing CAD-compatible, structurally valid output.
payload.reviewer_notes: Unreviewed arXiv preprint; authors explicitly note the methodology and presentation may change in revisions. No benchmark comparison against DeepCAD/BRepNet/Point2CAD/CAD-Recode/BrepGen is given in the excerpted text despite citing all of them as related work, so we cannot yet judge whether the reconstructed B-Reps are competitive in accuracy or compactness. The value to us is the symbolic geometry toolkit (PSPS splines, shape-preserving R-function CSG) as a possible verifier/utility primitive, not a directly transferable model architecture, since the task (point-cloud reverse engineering) differs from ours (program synthesis from an existing B-rep).

dependencies_on_other_methods: Pretrained Segment Anything Model (SAM), inherited from NeuSOGA
